title: Taurine ameliorates blood pressure and vascular function in patients with type 2 diabetes: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

sections.abstract:
Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) significantly elevates the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). The role of transient receptor potential canonical type 6 (TRPC6) channel mediated increased calcium entry have been identified on platelets from patients with T2D. It remains unknown whether taurine benefits vascular function in patients with T2D. Diabetic patients aged 60.0 ± 8.6 years in the taurine group, N = 82; and 59.1 ± 10.4 years in the placebo group, N = 83 were randomly enrolled and received either taurine (2.4 g/day) or placebo for 12 weeks. Compared to the placebo, taurine led to a significant reduction in systolic BP, and improvement of endothelium-dependent or -independent vasodilation and pulse wave velocity after taurine 12 weeks in patients with T2D. Taurine significantly inhibited the activation of platelet calcium influx in patients with T2D. Taurine may exert beneficial the effects on blood pressure and vascular dysfunction in patients with T2D.

Subject areas: Cardiovascular medicine, Dietary supplement
sections.introduction:
Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is a primary cause of nontraumatic amputations and significantly elevates the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with T2D. 1 , 2 Diabetes related cardiovascular complications including microangiopathy and macroangiopathy are major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with T2D. Early intervention can improve the incidence of PAD and related cardiovascular events in patients with T2D. Increased platelet activation represents the principal pathological mechanisms underlying diabetic PAD. In the context of hypertension, cytokines secreted during the inflammatory process stimulate megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, leading to the release of platelet precursors with an increased mean platelet volume into the bloodstream. 3 Recent findings indicate elevated mean platelet volume in patients with hypertensive crisis, 4 and both nondipper and dipper hypertensive patients exhibit a higher mean platelet volume than normotensive subjects. 5 , 6 A positive correlation exists between the mean platelet volume and systolic and diastolic blood pressure. 7 Mean platelet volume serves as a potential biomarker for the prognosis of cardiovascular diseases. Additionally, platelets in patients with T2D adhere more readily to the vascular endothelium and aggregate compared to those in healthy individuals. The increased platelet calcium influx is correlated with the vascular dysfunction observed in diabetic patients with PAD. 8

Both Taurine and H 2 S can be synthesized from methionine and cysteine. Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is a semi-essential amino acid and also as a nitrogen compound, which is derived from dietary sources in animal and marine foods, such as seafood, fish, dark poultry meat, breast milk, and eggs. Although eggs contain taurine are very low compared to these other sources. 9 H 2 S is a gas signaling molecule and its vasodilator effect has been widely studied in the cardiovascular system. 10 Epidemiological studies have shown that taurine may alleviate cardiovascular dysfunction, regulate glucose and lipid metabolism, 11 delay the development of atherosclerosis, 12 and ameliorate the pathogenesis of obesity and hypertension. 13 A lower dietary taurine content is observed in hypertensive patients. 14 In previous reports, we highlighted that taurine supplementation can lower blood pressure and improve endothelium-dependent and endothelium-independent vasodilation which is related to the increased plasma H 2 S and taurine concentrations in prehypertensive patients. 15 The direct impact of taurine on vascular functions may influence both vasoconstriction and vasodilation, involving calcium-dependent channels. 12 However, the effects of taurine supplementation on blood pressure and vascular function remain elusive in diabetic patients. Transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) channels, which have been identified on human platelets, 16 TRPC6 have been shown to mediate calcium influx into platelets in diabetic patients, related to hyperglycemia increases the expression of TRPC6 channels. 17 In this study, we investigated the effects of chronic taurine supplementation on blood pressure and vascular function in patients with T2D through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial and also explore its underlying mechanism.
sections.methods:
This single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted in accordance with the (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials, CONSORT) guidelines for the presentation of clinical trials (CONSORT 2010 Explanation and Elaboration) and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The clinical research program received approval from the Ethics Committee of Daping Hospital at the Army Medical University and was registered with clinicaltrials.gov (identifier: NCT03410537 ). Two hundred patients with T2D, aged 18–75 years, were recruited at Daping Hospital between January 2017 and January 2019. The exclusion criteria were patients with acute diabetic complications or thyroid disease, those unable to discontinue other drugs affecting metabolism, individuals who were allergic or contraindicated the drugs used in this study, those with severe cardiac dysfunction, those with liver or kidney failure, pregnant or lactating women, those planning pregnancy, and individuals participating in other clinical trials within the past 3 months before this trial. A total of 165 patients with diabetes were enrolled and randomly assigned to the placebo group ( n = 83, 36 males) or taurine group ( n = 82, 36 males), and 54 age-matched normal control subjects without taurine supplementation were enrolled only as baseline comparisons in the study. In addition, because of the number of cases, it was not possible to achieve grouping analysis by age. According to taurine pharmacokinetics, the plasma elimination half-life (T1/2) and the ratio of clearance/bioavailability (Cl/F) are 1.0 ± 0.3 h and 21.1 ± 7.8 L/h, respectively. 44 We used a fractional dose of taurine to maintain stable plasma taurine concentrations, corroborating the study of Zhang et al. 45 Baseline characteristics were collected at enrollment, and taurine supplementation were given at 2.4 g/d (0.8 g three times a day) or a placebo (0.8 g) three times a day. The study duration was 12 weeks, and all participants adhered to the intervention guidelines. Taurine supplementation and placebo made by Disha Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd, China.

The primary outcome measure was the alteration in brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) after 12 weeks. The secondary outcomes included changes in body weight, waist circumference (WC), blood pressure (BP), flow-mediated dilation (FMD), nitroglycerin-mediated dilation (NMD), carotid intima-media thickness (IMT), body mass index (BMI), glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), fasting blood glucose (FBG), triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and serum uric acid, which were measured by auto analyzer (Mairui, Shenzhen, China). Measurement of ankle brachial index (ABI) and toe brachial index (TBI). All measurements were performed after at least 30 min of acclimatization at a room temperature of 23°C–25°C, with the subject in a supine position. The ABI was determined as the ratio of ankle systolic BP to brachial systolic BP, with both BPs determined via an automatic Omron VP-2000/1000 device (Omron Healthcare, Kyoto, Japan).

All the participants signed an informed consent form before their voluntary participation. This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and the clinical research program was approved by the Ethics Committee of Daping Hospital at the Army Medical University. Clinical trial number: NCT03410537 .

Plasma hydrogen sulfide and taurine levels were measured before and after taurine or placebo supplementation via reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) after derivatization with excess monobromobimane (MBB) to form a stable sulfide-dibimane derivative2. Briefly, a total of 30 μL of plasma was mixed with 70 μL of 100 mmol/L Tris-HCl buffer (pH 9.5, 0.1 mmol/L DTPA), followed by the addition of 50 μL of 10 mmol/L MBB. The reaction was stopped after 30 min by adding 50 μL of 200 mmol/L 5-sulfosalicylic acid, the sample was subsequently centrifuged, and the supernatant was analyzed via a Shimadzu Prominence HPLC with fluorescence detection (λex: 390 nm and λem: 475 nm) and an Eclipse XDB-C18 column.

Flow-mediated (endothelium-dependent) and nitroglycerin-mediated (endothelium-independent) vasodilation were performed on the brachial artery at 4.5 cm above the antecubital fossa before inflation of a pneumatic cuff on the upper arm to 250 mm Hg for 5 min and at 1 min after cuff release by a single trained sonographer with high-resolution ultrasonography using a 7.5-MHz linear transducer on an HY 6000 system (Wuxi Haiying Electronic Medical System Co. Ltd., Jiangsu, China). 15 FMD was expressed as the percentage dilation from the baseline diameter to that observed at 1 min after cuff release. NMD was expressed as the percentage change from the baseline diameter to that observed after nitroglycerin administration.

Platelets were obtained from healthy control subjects or patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. All the donors provided informed consent. The subjects did not take antiplatelet drugs, including aspirin for at least 2 weeks. Platelets were extracted according to our previously described methods before and after taurine or placebo supplementation. 17 Centrifuge the blood at 240 g for 10 min to obtain platelet-rich plasma, and then centrifuge it again at 240 g for 15 min. Resuspend the platelets in Hanks balanced salt solution containing (mmol/L) NaCl 136, KCl 5.40, CaCl2 1, KH2PO4 0.44, Na2HPO4 0.34, N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N-2-ethanesulfonic acid 10, pH 7.4. Incubate the platelets with 1 mol/L fluorescent dye 1-[2-(5-carboxyoxazole-2-yl)-6-aminobenzofuran-5-oxo]-2-(2-amino-5-methylphenoxy)-ethane-N,N,N-triacetoxymethyltris(2-pyridylmethyl)triazine (fura2-AM; Invitrogen) for 60 min. Centrifuge the platelets at 240 g for 15 min and remove the external dye. Then, resuspend the platelet particles in the Hanks balanced salt solution. Adjust the platelet count to 1 × 108 platelets/mL. To exclude the effect of the separation procedure (including centrifugation and washing procedures) on platelets, we conducted additional experiments in which platelets were isolated in the presence of 25 mmol/L glucose. Subsequently, the platelets were exposed to 5.5 mmol/L glucose or 25 mmol/L glucose (including loading fura 2-AM).The changes in platelet-free Ca 2+ were measured via the Fura-2 a.m./Ca 2+ fluorescence probe technique and a fluorescence ratio meter (Fluoroskan Ascent Fluorometer, Thermo LabSystems Oy, Helsinki, Finland). 17

Human platelets were dissolved in extraction buffer containing 0.5 M Tris-HCl, 1% NP-40, 1% Triton X-100, 1 g/L SDS, 1.5 M NaCl, 0.2 M EDTA, 0.01 M EGTA, and protease and/or phosphatase inhibitors." The lysate was sonicated and cooled at −20°C for 20 min, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 × g for 20 min at 4°C. The resulting supernatant was collected and the protein concentration was quantified using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay. Equal amounts of protein (50 μg per lane) were separated by electrophoresis on a 10% SDS-polyacrylamide gel (SDS-PAGE). The primary antibodies used were, including TRPC6 (Alomone, Israel), SERCA2, SERCA3 (Santa Cruz, USA), STIM1 (Abcam), CaMKII (Abcam), and followed by incubated with the secondary antibodies (ZSGB-BIO). Original western blot images are available in this paper’s supplemental information ( Data S1 ).

The sample size was chosen to ensure 90% power to detect a 100% difference in baPWV, with a 2-sided significance level of 0.05 and an assumed dropout rate of 20%, according to previously published data and a preliminary trial of participants. 15 We anticipated a minimum between-group difference of 100 with a standard deviation of 200 for the change in baPWV from baseline to 12 weeks. Our initial target was a total sample size of 200 patients. Ultimately, we successfully enrolled 165 patients.

The participants were randomly assigned to receive either taurine or a placebo at a 1:1 allocation ratio via block randomization with a fixed block size. The randomization process was computer-generated, employing blocks of ten. A research assistant, who was not involved in the trial, executed the randomization in the patient’s presence. An independent researcher, who was uninvolved in the study and blinded to the treatment allocation, conducted the statistical analyses.

All patients exhibited good tolerance to taurine. There were no adverse events or dropouts related to taurine supplementation.

All statistical analyses adhered to the intention-to-treat principle (including patients who received at least one dose and participated in a random grouping), and the last follow-up results of lost cases were treated as missing data. Normally distributed data are presented as the means ± SD, SDs, whereas nonnormally distributed data are expressed as the medians (25th and 75th percentiles). The Mann‒Whitney test was used to compare continuous variables between the placebo and taurine groups, and the independent samples t-test was used to compare variables before and after treatment. Correlation analysis was performed via Spearman nonparametric correlation analysis. A significance level of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All the statistical analyses were conducted via SPSS 18.0.
sections.results:
All patients underwent comprehensive physical examinations, the results of which are detailed in Table S1 . Among the 200 patients screened in the study, a total of 165 were randomized, 144 of whom successfully completed the entire study protocol with complete data, resulting in a loss rate of 12.7% ( Figure S1 ). Both the taurine and placebo interventions were well tolerated, with no reports of serious adverse events from any of the participants. Compared with healthy control subjects, the enrolled patients with T2D had higher clinic BPs, WC, BMI, HBA1c, FBG, and increased baPWV at baseline. There were no significant differences at baseline characteristics between patients with T2D in the taurine and placebo groups.

Taurine supplementation in patients with T2D over 12 weeks of treatment resulted in a significant reduction in clinical SBP which was 7 mmHg lower (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.29–10.70; p < 0.05) than the corresponding baseline value. Furthermore, there was a significant decrease in plasma uric acid levels in the taurine group of patients with T2D after 12 weeks compared to their baseline values ( p < 0.05; Figure 1 C; Table S2 ). However, these changes did not differ in the placebo group of patients with T2D after 12 weeks of treatment ( Figures 1 A–1C).

Effects of taurine supplementation on blood pressure (BP)

(A–C) The clinical systolic BP (SBP, A), diastolic BP (DBP, B), and uric acid (C) of participants treated with taurine or placebo at baseline pretreatment (0 weeks, Pre) and after treatment (12 weeks, Post).

The data are presented as the means ± SDs. ∗ p < 0.05, compared with the respective pre- and post-treatment after 12 weeks of taurine supplementation. ns p > 0.05, ## p < 0.01, and # p < 0.05 compared with taurine supplementation post-treatment or placebo after 12 weeks. N = 66 in the taurine group and N = 78 in the placebo group.

After 12 weeks of taurine supplementation in patients with T2D, both endothelium-dependent vasodilation FMD and endothelium-independent vasodilation NMD significantly improved by 2.4% and 5.2%, respectively ( Figures 2 A and 2B). Additionally, a reliable marker of arterial stiffness, baPWV, significantly decreased after 12 weeks of taurine supplementation in patients with T2D ( Figure 2 C). However, no significant differences were observed in the placebo group of patients with T2D ( p > 0.05).

Effects of taurine supplementation on vasodilation and arterial stiffness

(A–C) Flow-mediated dilation (FMD; A), nitroglycerin-mediated dilation (NMD; B), and brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV; C) of participants treated with taurine or placebo at baseline pretreatment (0 weeks, Pre) and after treatment (12 weeks, Post).

The data are presented as the means ± SDs, ∗ p < 0.05, compared with the respective pre- and post-treatment values after 12 weeks of taurine supplementation # p < 0.05, ns p > 0.05 compared with treatment with taurine supplementation or placebo after 12 weeks. N = 66 in the taurine group and N = 78 in the placebo group.

To elucidate the underlying mechanisms of the effects of taurine on blood pressure and vascular function, we further examined changes in platelet Ca 2+ , plasma H 2 S, and taurine levels at baseline and after 12 weeks of treatment. The ABI and TBI were negatively correlated with changes in platelet Ca 2+ at baseline in patients with T2D ( Figures 3 A and 3B). After 12 weeks of treatment, the changes in platelet Ca 2+ were significantly decreased in the taurine group of patients with T2D ( Figure 3 C, p < 0.01). However, no significant differences in platelet Ca 2+ were detected in the placebo group of patients with T2D ( p > 0.05). Plasma H 2 S levels were significantly increased after 12 weeks of treatment in the taurine group of patients with T2D (43.3 ± 20.69 μmol/L at baseline to 88.3 ± 26.17 μmol/L after 12 weeks; p < 0.001); however, these changes were not observed (41.2 ± 33.71 μmol/L at baseline to 32.6 ± 16.46 μmol/L after 12 weeks; p > 0.05; Figure 3 D) in patients with T2D treated with placebo. Furthermore, plasma taurine levels at baseline were negatively correlated with baPWV, FBG, WC, and body weight in patients with T2D ( Figure S2 ). After 12 weeks treatment, plasma taurine levels were significantly increased in the taurine group of patients with T2D (58.2 ± 48.22 μmol/L at baseline to 89.1 ± 71.22 μmol/L after 12 weeks; p < 0.05); however, these changes were not observed in patients with T2D treated with placebo ( Figure 3 E).

Effects of taurine supplementation on platelet calcium, plasma H 2 S and taurien levels

(A and B) Correlations between changes in platelet calcium influx and the ankle-brachial index (ABI; A) or toe-brachial index (TBI; B) at baseline (V0) in the participants.

(C–E) Changes in platelet calcium influx (C) and plasma levels of H 2 S (D) and taurine (E) at baseline (Pre) and after (Post) treatment with placebo or taurine supplementation for 12 weeks. The data are presented as the means ± SDs, ns p > 0.05, ∗ p < 0.05, ∗∗∗ p < 0.001, compared with the Pre and Post groups. N = 21–41.

We then investigated the mechanism responsible for the effects of taurine supplementation on platelet calcium in patients with T2D. The administration of high levels of glucose significantly increased the protein expression of TRPC6, CAMKII, STIM1, SERCA2, and SERCA3 in platelets from healthy control subjects in a dose- and time-dependent manner ( Figures 4 A and 4B). Furthermore, the administration of the H 2 S donor NaHS reversed these effects of high glucose on platelets ( Figures 5 A and 5B). Importantly, in platelets from patients with T2D, the protein expression levels of TRPC6, CAMKII, STIM1, SERCA2, and SERCA3 were significantly elevated compared with those in platelets from healthy control subjects ( Figure 6 A).

Effects of high glucose conditions on TRPC6, SERCA2, SERCA3, STIM1, and CaMKII

(A and B) The protein expression levels of TRPC6, SERCA2, SERCA3, STIM1, and CaMKII in the presence of high glucose (15, 25, and 35 mmol/L) plus thapsigargin (TG 1 μmol/L) in a dose-dependent (A) and time-dependent (B) manner in platelets from healthy control individuals.

The data are presented as the means ± SDs. ∗ p < 0.05,∗∗ p < 0.01, and ∗∗∗ p < 0.001, vs. the control (Cont) without high glucose treatment.

Effects of high glucose and taurine on TRPC6, SERCA2, SERCA3, STIM1, and CaMKII

(A and B) The protein expression levels of TRPC6, SERCA2, SERCA3, STIM1, and CaMKII in platelets from healthy control individuals treated with high glucose (25 mmol/L) or high glucose plus NaHS (40 mmol/L) were detected via western blotting (A). The data were quantified from bands from three independent immunoblots, and the relative expression levels are shown (B).

The data are presented as the means ± SDs. ∗ p < 0.05,∗∗ p < 0.01, vs. high glucose treatment.

SERCA2, TRPC6, SERCA3, STIM1, and CaMKII proteins in patients with T2D and healthy control individuals (NT)

(A–E) The protein expression levels of STIM1 (A), TRPC6 (B), CaMKII (C), SERCA2 (D),and SERCA3 (E) in patients with T2D and healthy control individuals (NT).

(F) The data were quantified from bands from three independent immunoblots, and the relative expression levels are shown. The data are presented as the means ± SDs. ∗ p < 0.05, ∗∗ p < 0.01, and ∗∗∗ p < 0.001, compared with the NT group. The data were quantified from bands from three independent immunoblots, and the relative expression levels are shown.
sections.discussion:
The main findings of the present study revealed that taurine supplementation for 12 weeks significantly improved blood pressure and vascular dysfunction in patients with T2D. Additionally, increased platelet Ca 2+ influx was correlated with the ABI and TBI in patients with T2D. Taurine supplementation substantially decreases platelet Ca 2+ , but elevates plasma H 2 S and taurine levels in patients with T2D. However, these beneficial effects were not detected in patients with T2D treated with placebo. In experimental studies, we demonstrated that high glucose increased platelet TRPC6, CAMKII, STIM1, SERCA2, and SERCA3 protein expression, which was reversed by the administration of the H 2 S donor NaHS. The protein expression levels of TRPC6, CAMKII, STIM1, SERCA2, and SERCA3 were significantly elevated in platelets from patients with T2D compared with those in platelets from healthy control subjects. Our findings indicate that taurine supplementation may be a promising intervention for diabetes-related vascular dysfunction through the improvement of platelet calcium handling.

Taurine derives directly from the host’s diets, in highest amounts from meat and seafood and to a lower extent from algae and plants, 18 but also liberated by microbial bile salt hydrolases from endogenously produced taurine-conjugated bile acids. 19 Both the endogenous flux of taurine production and the exogenous taurine intake from diet have not been exactly quantified to date, though the metabolites of the taurine pathway have been elucidated. Taurine is widely distributed in human tissues, and in some tissues taurine concentration is much higher than that in plasma, 20 such as in retina photoreceptor cells can reach up to 70 mmol. 21 The sources of intracellular taurine are divided into endogenous synthesis and exogenous dietary intake. Rana SK found that taurine was absent from the vegans diet and taurine was 463 ± 156 (umol/L) in omnivores, but plasma taurine concentration were no significantly difference between vegans and omnivores. 22 The body primarily maintains taurine concentrations through dietary intake because endogenous synthesis is constrained. 23

About the effects of taurine supplementation on plasma taurine levels, some studies showed that dietary taurine no effect on plasma taurine levels. Bellentani S showed that taurine supplementation to hamsters increased taurine content in liver and in urine but did not affect plasma taurine. In addition, taurine inhibited methionine uptake in intestinal Caco-2 cells. This inhibitory effect occurs because taurine and methionine share the same transporter. 24 This may explain why dietary taurine may reduce the high plasma methionine levels which induced by dietary methionine. This inhibitory effect occurs on the apical side of the intestine without an increase in plasma taurine. 25 However, Suliman ME showed that patients with end-stage renal disease, taurine supplementation (100 mg/kg per day) lead to extremely high plasma taurine levels. 26 In current study we showed that a significant increase in plasma taurine levels after 12 weeks taurine supplementation in patients with T2D. But not all the patients with T2D increased their plasma taurine levels after 12 weeks taurine supplementation. This absence of an effect of taurine supplements on plasma taurine levels possibly does not exclude an increase in taurine levels in extravascular or intracellular compartments. 27

Taurine, an essential β-amino acid, has been demonstrated to have regulatory effects on various biological processes, including antioxidation, anti-inflammatory responses, anti-atherosclerotic activity, and metabolic improvement. 12 , 13 DiNicolantonio J reported that endogenous production of H 2 S via taurine supplementation rose a virtual doubling of plasma H 2 S. 10 However, it remains unclear whether taurine supplementation benefits vascular dysfunction in patients with T2D. In this study, we demonstrated that the plasma H 2 S levels were significantly increased by 51% after 12 weeks of taurine supplementation in patients with T2D. Taurine effects can be independent from plasma taurine levels although they are taurine mediated, these exerted through H 2 S or intracellular taurine effects. We showed that administration of a low dose of taurine for 12 weeks can improve vascular dysfunction, which is correlated with increased plasma H 2 S and taurine levels in patients with T2D. A recent crossover study revealed that taurine can reverse early vascular abnormalities and enhance endothelial function in type 1 diabetes mellitus patients. 28 Furthermore, animal experiments demonstrated that taurine could ameliorate streptozotocin-induced endothelial dysfunction by suppressing the expression of lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor-1 (LOX-1) and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1). Our study showed that there were no significant associations between plasma taurine and H 2 S, blood pressures and platelets calcium influx. In addition, not all patients with T2D who received taurine supplementation had an increase in plasma taurine levels. The plasma taurine responses can vary between individual, for example in dependence on their kidney function or gut microbiome. Taurine effects exerted through H 2 S or via intracellular taurine can be independent from plasma taurine levels although they are taurine-mediated.

baPWV is widely recognized as biomarker for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). 29 Hiroyasu et al. 30 investigated 102 healthy young students and reported that acute administration of taurine decreased BP and HR, and attenuated baPWV. In this study, we demonstrated that taurine supplementation significantly improved baPWV and decreased plasma uric acid levels in patients with T2D. A prior study reported that oral taurine improved insulin sensitivity and beta cell function in obese and overweight nondiabetic men, 31 contributing to the amelioration of glucose homeostasis and islet function. 32 Haidari et al. 33 reported that taurine supplementation with a weight-loss diet has a greater effect on the lipid profile and metabolic risk factors. Zhang et al. 34 showed that taurine has a beneficial effect on serum lipids in overweight or obese individuals, and improves subcutaneous white adipose tissue plasticity in obese women. 35 Furthermore, taurine can modulate metabolic processes involved in obesity through impacting peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor- Gamma coactivator 1 Alpha (PGC-1α) regulation of energy metabolism, 36 and taurine activating silent information regulator 2 homolog 1 (SIRT1)/AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) regulates lipid metabolism. 37 Recently, Hou et al. 38 reported that the taurine transporter regulates adipocyte formation through the transport of amino acids and may serve as a target for the therapeutic intervention of obesity.

Platelet hyperactivity plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of ASCVD. Endothelial dysfunction induced by hyperglycemia increases platelet Ca 2+ , rendering platelets more vulnerable and prone to activation. 39 Therefore, antiplatelet therapy is routinely recommended for ASCVD management. 40 Our previous work demonstrated elevated platelet Ca 2+ levels in patients with T2D, particularly those with T2D with PAD or hypertension. 17 In this study, we first demonstrated that changes in platelet Ca 2+ were negatively correlated with the ABI and TBI in patients with T2D. SERCA2 in the dense tubular system and SERCA3 in lysosome-like acidic organelles mediate the reuptake of Ca 2+ to maintain cytosolic Ca 2+ homeostasis. However, overexpressed SERCA may exacerbate Ca 2+ overload by activating store-operated calcium entry (SOCE). 41 In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, we showed that the administration of taurine (2.4 g per day) for 12 weeks, significantly decreased SOCE-mediated platelet Ca 2+ , but had no effect on the placebo group in patients with T2D. Importantly, high levels of glucose elevated the protein expression of calcium-handling-related molecules, such as SERCA2, SERCA3, STIM1, and CAMKII in platelets from healthy controls, and these calcium-handling-related molecules were markedly upregulated in platelets from patients with T2D compared with those from healthy controls. Targeting platelet Ca 2+ may be a promising approach to counteract diabetic vascular dysfunction.

TRPCs play a significant role in the pathogenesis of diabetes and hypertension. 42 Specifically, TRPC6 mediates SOCE by regulating phosphatidylinositol-4, 5-bisphosphate (PIP2), a precursor of inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) that binds with IP3R to promote Ca 2+ release. 43 The TRPC6-mediated increase in platelet Ca 2+ influx and subsequent Ca 2+ overload could be a contributing factor to platelet activation. In this study, the administration of high levels of glucose elevated TRPC6 protein expression in platelets from healthy controls. Notably, taurine administration has been shown to increase H 2 S production by increasing the expression of CSE and CBS. 15 In this study, we demonstrated that taurine supplementation led to a 2.03-fold increase in plasma H 2 S levels and a 1.53-fold increase in taurine levels in patients with T2D after 12 weeks of intervention. Furthermore, the administration of NaHS, an H 2 S donor, markedly attenuated the high glucose-induced upregulation of the protein expression of TRPC6 and calcium-handling-related molecules in platelets. These findings suggest that taurine mitigates platelet activation by inhibiting high glucose elevated TRPC6-induced Ca 2+ overload in patients with T2D.

The study was conducted in a single-center and involved a relatively small sample size. Long-term follow-up trial is imperative to substantiate the observed beneficial effects in diabetic patients with PAD. Moreover, it is important to acknowledge that the impact of taurine supplementation on the activation of the sympathetic system and increased urinary norepinephrine, and epinephrine excretion that could affect improvements in blood pressure cannot be ruled out.
sections.limitations: The study was conducted in a single-center and involved a relatively small sample size. Long-term follow-up trial is imperative to substantiate the observed beneficial effects in diabetic patients with PAD. Moreover, it is important to acknowledge that the impact of taurine supplementation on the activation of the sympathetic system and increased urinary norepinephrine, and epinephrine excretion that could affect improvements in blood pressure cannot be ruled out.
